## Chapter Summary

Data preparation transforms data from the form in which it was recorded into the form an analysis needs, and in accounting it usually means bringing attributes that live in related tables onto the transactions being analyzed. Because a preparation error changes every number that follows without announcing itself, every preparation step should be paired with a check, such as a count of unmatched rows or a total that must agree with its source, and the whole procedure should be documented so that someone else can repeat it.

Text functions extract, standardize, and validate text fields. MID, LEFT, RIGHT, FIND, and LEN extract the parts of a structured value, such as the product type in a Charles River item code. TRIM, CLEAN, SUBSTITUTE, UPPER, LOWER, and PROPER standardize text, but they should be applied only after a test shows that a field needs them, because standardizing clean data can damage it, as PROPER does to names such as Donaldson LLC. Date functions assign transactions to fiscal periods and measure the time between events. Charles River's fiscal year is the calendar year, a non-calendar fiscal year needs an adjusted quarter formula, and a fixed as-of date is more reliable than TODAY for any measure of age.

Lookup functions retrieve a value from one table using a key from another. XLOOKUP is the most flexible, INDEX and MATCH work in every version of Excel, and VLOOKUP, the oldest, is limited to keys in the first column. A lookup is correct when it follows a relationship toward its "one" side, and it returns only the first match when it follows a relationship toward the "many" side, where MINIFS, SUMIFS, and COUNTIFS are the right tools. Counting the rows a lookup failed to match is the first check on any lookup. Preparation also distinguishes blanks that record a fact, such as a missing PromotionID on a line with no promotion, from blanks that mean information is missing, and it tests whether values are valid for their purpose, as the fractional quantities on items sold by the unit are not.

Power Query performs the same preparation as a recorded, refreshable procedure. A merge combines two queries on a key column, with a join kind, usually left outer, that decides which rows appear, and custom columns calculate new values with Power Query's formula language. Applied to the Charles River data, these tools produced InvoiceLines, a single table in which every invoice line carries its fiscal period, product group and type, and customer segment. Its totals agree with the source and with the lookups, and preparing it showed that many lines of the Furniture Seasonal Promotion were invoiced after the promotion ended.
